entities.name: Marcus Gavius Apicius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marcus Gavius Apicius, a legendary Roman epicure and connoisseur of luxury, flourished in the 1st century CE during the principate of Emperor Tiberius (14–37 CE). His name became synonymous with extravagant dining and refined tastes, cementing his place in historical memory not merely as a person, but as an archetype of Roman gourmandise. While the precise details of his life remain somewhat shrouded by time and anecdote, his enduring legacy is inextricably linked to the *Apicius* cookbook, a compilation of Roman recipes that, though likely not penned by him directly, carries his name and reputation for culinary excellence.

Apicius was renowned for his opulent lifestyle and seemingly boundless expenditures on food and entertainment. Seneca the Younger, in his *Consolation to Helvia*, and Pliny the Elder, in his *Natural History*, both recount tales of Apicius's legendary excesses, including his invention of a method to fatten pigs with figs to enhance their livers and his purported journey to Libya in search of a particularly large species of prawn. The Greek grammarian Apion even dedicated a lost work, *On the Luxury of Apicius*, to his fabled indulgences, suggesting his notoriety was widespread. His life reportedly concluded in 37 CE by suicide after he squandered his vast fortune of 100 million sesterces on lavish banquets, finding himself with only 10 million sesterces remaining—an amount he deemed insufficient for his accustomed standard of living.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Marcus Gavius Apicius's name, though perhaps more of a symbol than a direct author, is indelibly tied to the preservation of Roman culinary knowledge through the *Apicius* cookbook, which continues to inform studies of ancient gastronomy. His legendary life also serves as a potent illustration of Roman elite luxury and social values.
